b: The US Trustee has asked the judge overseeing Character.ai's bankruptcy to refuse lead-bidder status to Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC, the buyer the company picked to pay $10 million for its app, AI models and user data, because the filing that named the buyer never said who stands behind it. In an objection filed on Thursday, November 19, 2026, in the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware, Andrew R. Vara, the US Trustee for Regions 3 and 9, said Character Technologies, Inc. "failed to follow the procedures for designating the additional stalking horse purchaser" by leaving out the parent or sponsor of a company formed the day before it was chosen. The objection, Docket No. 202, asks the court to deny both the designation and the bid protections attached to it. A hearing is set for 2 p.m. on Monday, November 23, the day before bids are due.

The US government's bankruptcy watchdog wants a judge to refuse Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC its place as the opening bidder for Character.ai's app, AI models and users' chats, because the company never disclosed who owns or funds the buyer, which was set up in Delaware the day before it was chosen. The court's own sale rules required that disclosure for any newly formed buyer, and the US Trustee argues that without it the states, creditors and business partners who had four days to object could not judge who would end up holding the platform and its advertising data. If the judge agrees on November 23, Smirks and Pangs would be denied that protected position and the $350,000 payment it was promised if outbid. Character.ai asked the same afternoon for permission to keep the backer's name out of public filings, describing it only as a New York venture capital fund.

The objection runs to five pages. Linda J. Casey, a trial attorney in the Justice Department's Office of the United States Trustee in Wilmington, signed it on Vara's behalf. Its target is the "Notice of Designation of Additional Stalking Horse Purchaser and Stalking Horse Supplement for Assets Other Than the Disney Target Assets," the November 14 filing in which Character Technologies named Smirks and Pangs as the stalking horse for everything outside Disney's license, at $10 million in cash plus certain liabilities, as PPC Land reported when Character.ai users' chats faced a $10m sale to Smirks and Pangs.
The preliminary statement makes the whole case in four sentences:

"The Debtor sought authority to designate additional stalking horse purchasers subsequent to this Court's approval of bid procedures. The Debtor failed to follow the procedures for designating the additional stalking horse purchaser. This failure is not merely technical but impacts the ability of parties to evaluate the transaction and raise timely objections. As such, the Court should not authorize the designation of the additional stalking horse purchaser or approve the requested bid protections."

Standing comes from two statutes. Under 28 U.S.C. § 586(a)(3), the US Trustee "is charged with administrative oversight of the bankruptcy system in this District," and under 11 U.S.C. § 307 it "has standing to be heard on the issues raised in this pleading," according to the filing. It cites the Third Circuit's 2003 decision in United Artists Theatre Co. v. Walton, which held that US Trustees "protect the public interest by aiding bankruptcy judges in monitoring certain aspects of bankruptcy proceedings," and a 1994 decision involving Columbia Gas describing the office's "public interest standing," which "goes beyond mere pecuniary interest." A 1977 House report, also cited, said US Trustees "serve as bankruptcy watch-dogs to prevent fraud, dishonesty, and overreaching in the bankruptcy arena."

The objection is the first filed against the Smirks and Pangs designation. Its caption gives the US Trustee its own deadline, 9 p.m. on November 19, a day later than the 9 p.m. November 18 cutoff that applied to other parties. When 35 states and the District of Columbia served deposition topics on the company on November 19, PPC Land noted that no objection to the designation had appeared on the docket by the November 18 deadline, in coverage of how Character.ai faces 35 states' questions under oath on users' data. The filing does not explain why the US Trustee's deadline differed.

There is also a stray reference in the caption, which reads "Re: D.I. 165." Docket No. 165 is a motion for the pro hac vice admission of Rebecca L. Epstein of Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati, filed on November 16, according to the court docket. The body of the objection, and the docket entry for it, tie the filing to Docket No. 164, the designation notice.
The rule the notice left out

The case turns on what the bidding procedures order demanded. The court entered that order on November 4, 2026, as Docket No. 106. Character Technologies had filed its bid procedures motion on October 13, the day after its petition, and the court shortened notice and set the hearing for October 30, according to the objection.

The order let the company name one or more additional stalking horse purchasers "on or before November 14, 2026." A company chosen that way would be announced through an "Additional Stalking Horse Supplement" seeking authority to enter into the purchase agreement, "subject to final approval at the sale hearing," and to grant bid protections, according to the filing. One item had to be in it. "The Additional Stalking Horse Supplement had to include certain information including, if the stalking horse purchaser is a newly formed entity, its parent company or sponsor," the US Trustee wrote, citing paragraph 4 of the order.

That requirement was already in the revised order the company submitted on November 3, which also replaced a three-day hearing with a written deadline and provided that a designation nobody objected to would be deemed approved without further notice or a hearing, as PPC Land reported when the judge said he would overrule 40 states' objections to Character.ai's Disney sale rules.
The facts, as the objection lays them out, are brief:

"The Debtor filed the Additional Stalking Horse Supplement on November 14, 2026. The supplement identified Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC as the stalking horse purchaser. This entity was formed on November 13, 2026."
"The Additional Stalking Horse Supplement does not disclose the purchaser's parent or sponsor, as required by the Procedures Order."

The November 14 notice did say other things. It gave the price, a termination payment of 3.5%, or $350,000, a list of 55 contracts the buyer would take over and a statement that Smirks and Pangs had no connection to the company other than through the agreement itself, as PPC Land reported on November 15. According to Delaware's Division of Corporations, the buyer was formed on November 13 under file number 10840241, with United Corporate Services, Inc. of Dover as registered agent, and the state's record lists no members or managers.

Speed is the second half of the argument. "Objections to the designation of the stalking horse purchaser, and the bid protections to be provided to them if they are outbid, were required to be filed just four days after the Additional Stalking Horse Supplement was filed," the objection says. The supplement went in on a Saturday, and the deadline fell on the following Wednesday evening, leaving three business days by PPC Land's count.

The US Trustee does not attack the mechanism itself. "These procedures afford a debtor flexibility to find stalking horse purchasers for some or all of its assets after entry of a bid procedures order," the filing says. "The procedures, however, require meaningful notice so parties can determine whether an objection is appropriate."
The heart of the objection is paragraph 17:

"The failure to provide the identity of the parent or sponsor behind a newly-formed purchaser prevents parties from being able to evaluate the proposed transaction and determine if an objection is appropriate. When granted permission to obtain approval of the designation of a stalking horse bidder and bid protections to be accorded thereto without a motion and on an expedited timeframe, providing the necessary information for parties to evaluate the transaction and raise appropriate objections is required. As such, the designation of the additional stalking horse purchaser should be denied."

What is not in the objection matters as well. It does not challenge the $10 million price, the size of the $350,000 payment, the list of assets or the treatment of users' data. It is a procedural objection, built on a single missing disclosure.
Why contract partners have a stake

Paragraphs 10 and 11 explain who loses most from the gap. Companies whose contracts the debtor may hand to a buyer were served with notice of possible assumption and assignment on November 4, 2026. Under the order, the timing of their objections depends on what kind of buyer ends up with the contract.

According to paragraph 24 of the order, as quoted in the objection, once the auction results are announced, parties may raise objections "solely with respect to the conduct of the Auction, the Winning Bidder (only if not a Stalking Horse Purchaser), modifications to any Stalking Horse Agreement, and adequate assurance of future performance by a Winning Bidder other than any Stalking Horse Purchaser." The approved contract notice, Exhibit 3 to the order, spells out the consequence:

"Any objections to adequate assurance of future performance by Disney or any other Additional Stalking Horse Purchaser designated by the Debtor shall also be filed by the Contract Objection Deadline. Any objections to adequate assurance of future performance by a Winning Bidder other than Disney or any other Additional Stalking Horse Purchaser designated by the Debtor shall be due at or prior to the Sale Hearing."

In plain terms, designation moves the clock. A counterparty facing an ordinary winning bidder can question that bidder's ability to perform as late as the sale hearing. A counterparty facing a stalking horse has to do it by the earlier contract deadline, and in this case without knowing who owns the company that would take over its contract.

The Smirks and Pangs list covers 55 contracts, seven of them with cure amounts that total $2,684,462 by PPC Land's calculation from the November 14 schedule. DigitalOcean's contract accounts for $2,646,136 of that. A supplemental notice of possible assumption and assignment, tied to the designation, followed on November 16 as Docket No. 178. DigitalOcean filed a limited objection and reservation of rights to the November 4 contract notice on November 18, as Docket No. 193, according to the docket. The US Trustee's filing does not mention either.
What is known about the buyer

The public record on Smirks and Pangs has grown since November 14, though not on the point the US Trustee raises. The signed purchase agreement, filed on November 16, carries the signature of Kai McPheeters as an authorized signatory for the buyer, a notice address on Broadway in Albany, New York, and a copy line to Eric E. Walker of Cooley LLP in Chicago. It requires a $1 million deposit and sets a December 31 outside date, as PPC Land reported when Character.ai's $10m sale was shown to hinge on moving chats without further consent. The same agreement refers to a confidentiality agreement signed on November 4 by an unnamed affiliate of the buyer, nine days before the buyer was formed. On November 15, PPC Land asked Wilson Sonsini, the company's counsel, who owns and controls Smirks and Pangs and who is funding the purchase price.
Character.ai's answer, filed the same afternoon

Character Technologies filed its own motion on the subject later on November 19, as Docket No. 203. It asks the court to let the company keep the identity of the buyer's financial sponsor out of the supplement and other public filings, relying on sections 105(a) and 107(b) of the Bankruptcy Code and Bankruptcy Rule 9018, according to the motion. The motion says the sponsor's name was withheld at the buyer's request because of commercial sensitivity, and describes the sponsor as a New York venture capital fund that invests in technology and software companies.

The motion also says the company had already disclosed the sponsor, confidentially, to the US Trustee, to proposed counsel for the creditors' committee and to counsel for the NAAG Client States. It proposes that the name go only to the court, the committee, the NAAG Client States and the US Trustee, plus any other party the court orders. Florida and Texas, both of which have objected in the case, are not among the states listed in the motion's footnote defining that group, and contract counterparties are not on the list either. As an alternative, the company asks the court to amend paragraph 4 of the bidding procedures order to delete the parent-or-sponsor requirement, a change it calls non-material.

The two filings talk past each other. The US Trustee's objection does not say whether the office knows who the sponsor is, and the company's motion does not mention the objection. Its notice sets the motion for the same 2 p.m. hearing on November 23 before Judge Brendan L. Shannon, with responses allowed at or before the hearing.

According to the objection, the bidding procedures order sets out the following path for naming an additional stalking horse purchaser:
The company may designate one or more additional stalking horse purchasers for assets other than those Disney is acquiring, "on or before November 14, 2026" (paragraph 7).

If it does, it files an "Additional Stalking Horse Supplement" by November 14, seeking authority to enter into the agreement, subject to final approval at the sale hearing, and to grant bid protections (paragraph 8).

The supplement goes to the US Trustee, the Consultation Parties, everyone known or reasonably believed to have expressed interest in acquiring all or a substantial portion of the assets within a year before the petition date, non-debtor counterparties to contracts proposed for assignment, "the attorneys general for each of the states," and parties that filed requests for notice (paragraph 8).
The supplement must include certain information, including the parent company or sponsor if the purchaser is a newly formed entity (paragraph 9, citing paragraph 4 of the order).

Objections to the designation and to the proposed bid protections are due four days after the supplement is filed (paragraph 15). Under the order as PPC Land reported it on November 4, a designation with no objection is deemed approved without further notice or a hearing, and an objection leads the company to ask the court for a hearing on an emergency basis.

Contract counterparties must file objections to adequate assurance of future performance by an additional stalking horse purchaser by the Contract Objection Deadline. Objections concerning any other winning bidder, apart from Disney, are due at or before the sale hearing (paragraphs 10 and 11, citing paragraph 24 and Exhibit 3 of the order).
The agreement remains subject to final approval at the sale hearing (paragraph 8).

The assets in play are not abstract. The Smirks and Pangs schedule covers the Character.ai website and apps, all AI models and weights, users' account information and chat content, advertising and analytics data, records of consents and advertising opt-outs, and the accounts the company uses to earn money from third-party ads, as PPC Land reported on November 15. Whoever controls the buyer would hold the conversations users have had with Character.ai's companion chatbot characters, together with the ad data built around them. The Consumer Federation of America has argued that such chats could be used to serve advertisements and that data brokers and advertising technology companies pose a particular risk, as PPC Land reported in What the therapist bot heard: Character.ai's chats are on the block.

The US Trustee has stepped in on the sale terms before. The office objected on November 13 to the investment banker's fee, as PPC Land reported when Character.ai's banker faced objection to a $2.05m fee on the $20m Disney sale. On October 29, 39 states and DC joined its call for a privacy ombudsman, as covered in 39 states and DC say Character.ai user data needs a privacy ombudsman. The court ordered one on November 17, as PPC Land reported when Character.ai faced a privacy ombudsman before its users' data can be sold, and the US Trustee appointed Lucy L. Thomson to the role the next day, at $650 an hour, as covered in Character.ai's planned data sale gets a $650-an-hour privacy ombudsman. A consumer privacy ombudsman reports on the privacy effects of a sale; the company's confidentiality motion does not list the ombudsman among those who would receive the sponsor's name.

The states have moved more slowly on the second buyer. Their 32-page objection of November 18 concerned the Disney license alone, as PPC Land reported when 39 states and DC asked the court to deny Disney's $20m Character.ai deal. Their first filing to name Smirks and Pangs, the November 19 deposition notice, asked among other things whether the models it would buy can reproduce or reveal users' personal information.

For Character Technologies, which is running its business as a debtor in possession, the timing is tight. The hearing falls the day before bids are due and eight days before the auction. If the judge denies the designation, Smirks and Pangs would not have the protected opening position or the $350,000 payment; the objection does not say whether the company could still bid as an ordinary bidder. If the judge grants the company's motion, or deletes the requirement from the order, the sponsor's name would stay out of the public record, and the fate of the designation would be decided at the same hearing.

The objection leaves several things unsaid. It does not name the sponsor, does not say whether the US Trustee was told the name privately, does not explain why the office's deadline ran a day past everyone else's and does not ask for the sponsor's identity to be disclosed as an alternative to denial. No other party had joined it on the docket by the morning of November 20.

Who: Andrew R. Vara, the US Trustee for Regions 3 and 9, through trial attorney Linda J. Casey, objecting against Character Technologies, Inc., the operator of Character.ai, and its chosen buyer, Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC. Contract counterparties, state attorneys general and creditors are the parties the US Trustee says were left unable to evaluate the deal.

What: An objection (Docket No. 202) asking the court to deny the designation of Smirks and Pangs as additional stalking horse purchaser for the assets outside Disney's license, and to deny its bid protections, because the designation notice did not disclose the parent or sponsor of a buyer formed the day before it was chosen, as the bidding procedures order required. The company responded the same day with a motion to keep the sponsor's identity confidential or to remove the requirement.

When: Filed on Thursday, November 19, 2026. The hearing is set for November 23 at 2 p.m., the day before the November 24 bid deadline, with the auction on December 1 and the sale hearing on December 3 and 4.
Where: The US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware, Case No. 26-11603 (BLS), before Judge Brendan L. Shannon.

Why: The US Trustee argues that the expedited designation process depends on meaningful notice, and that without the sponsor's name parties could not decide within four days whether to object. For contract counterparties, stalking horse status also moves forward the deadline to question the buyer's ability to perform. For the marketing community, the outcome bears on who would control Character.ai's user chats, advertising data and ad monetization accounts.
